target_customer: Large law firms and in-house legal teams doing transactional work (M&A, finance, real estate)
problem: Lawyers spend many hours drafting and negotiating contracts from precedent, with high risk of error and poor access to past deals at drafting time. Draftwise suggests language and playbooks from the firm's own knowledge base.
business_model: Enterprise SaaS sold to law firms by seat or firm-wide license
product_category: Legal AI for contract drafting, review and negotiation

founders.name: James Ding
founders.background_notes: Company bio says he spent a decade leading AI teams at Palantir and holds patents in data security and machine learning.

founders.name: Emre Ozen
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as ex-Palantir.

founders.name: Ozan Yalti
founders.background_notes: From the Series A post on the company blog. Another directory lists his title as CTO, conflicting with the YC page.

competitors.name: Kira Systems
competitors.what: Machine learning software that extracts information from contracts, used for review and diligence
competitors.traction_then: Customers included a majority of the world's leading law firms per the 2018 announcement
competitors.funding_then: 50M USD from Insight Venture Partners in September 2018, its first outside funding (called a Series A)

technical_complexity.rationale: Reliable contract drafting suggestions from precedent need document understanding, firm-specific knowledge indexing and strict security for law firms, which was hard for a small team in 2020 before large language models.

defensibility.rationale: Each firm's own precedent and playbooks become embedded, and law firm customers are sticky, but later broad legal AI platforms compete for the same workflows.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent absorbed Draftwise through 2026. Broader legal AI platforms later emerged as rivals, but they came after the batch.

market_need_then: TechCrunch's August 2020 demo day coverage said Draftwise claimed it could cut credit agreement drafting from about 30 hours to 10, had nearly half a dozen letters of intent from law firms and expected to charge big law firms over 500K USD a year.

identity.voice_and_tone: professional and precise, with coined product names like Ontonomi and Playbook Studio

branding.brand_signature: Ontonomi, the legal ontology product launched in 2026 with Ropes & Gray and Jones Day as partners
branding.community_and_virality: Law firm partnerships and a blog post titled I Am a Forward-Deployed CEO; no merch or community evidence found.

brand_strength.rationale: Law firm adoption is the main brand asset and press covers funding and partnerships, not the brand itself. The name is a descriptive compound.

outcome_analysis: Draftwise combined ex-Palantir engineers with a Stanford-trained former Clifford Chance lawyer and sold to big law with strategic law firm backing: Orrick joined the 2023 seed and Mishcon de Reya, Jones Day and Ropes & Gray later became partners. It raised a 5M USD seed in June 2023 and a 20M USD Series A led by Index in March 2024 after a long period without public rounds. No later round, exit or shutdown is reported through late 2026.
notes: Total raised about 25M USD (sum of two rounds, not stated by the company). Funding from 2020 to 2023 before the seed is unknown. A TechCrunch demo day line said a founder is a lawyer; this matches Yalti per the Series A post but TechCrunch did not name him. The seed post was found via search and not opened; its lead (Earlybird) and Orrick participation are also in Law.com and Legaltechnology coverage. The Series A post gives Index as lead and says YC and Earlybird are existing investors. Luminance is a probable rival but its dated pre-batch sources were not found, so it is only in takeover incumbents. Outcome searches found no layoffs or sale.
